To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the genetic contribution to aging is a multifactorial process that results from an interplay between stochastic events and the epistatic effects of deleterious and helpful genes.
deleterious and helpful genes define life expectancy

1) the genetic pool in which deleterious and helpful genes interact in a constant epigenetic relationship defines the life expectancy; 2) the genetic pool is the result of an evolutionary process; 3) the evolutionary process is a result of natural selection and random mutations that are influenced by the environment; 4) the evolutionary process results in a set of alleles that are beneficial to the organism; 5) those alleles that confer disease resistance are longevity‐enabling and are beneficial
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of the genetic contribution to the process of aging and longevity.
the identification of the genes that affect human aging and with the elucidation of the mechanisms that underlie the aging process.
understanding the role of genetic factors in the development of age‐related disease and the genetic basis of human longevity.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
genetic factors are important in determining longevity, but that the effect of genes is not deterministic and is modified by environmental influences.
the genes that predispose to early disease and death are deleterious and that those that are protective are helpful, but the genes that are responsible for the aging process per se remain elusive.
genetic variation in human populations is responsible for the differences in life expectancy.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
aging is a complex genetic trait with multiple genetic and environmental influences that are modulated by epistatic interactions and by stochastic events.
the aging process is the result of a complex interaction of genes and environment.

the genetic pool in which the genes with deleterious effects on aging (those that shorten life) interact with those with a beneficial effect (longevity genes) in a constant and complex epistatic relationship results in the modulation of the final phenotypic expression under particular environmental conditions.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the genes that are associated with the aging process can be divided into two categories, those that promote longevity and those that shorten the life course, and that these genes can be found in both humans and model organisms.
the genetic pool of a population, which is constantly being modified by natural selection and random drift, has a major influence on life expectancy.
we must consider the genetic background of individuals when we are trying to understand the process of aging and its relationship to health and longevity.
